{{Short description|Empirical model for microorganisms growth limited by a nutrient}}
The '''Monod equation''' is a [[mathematical model]] for the growth of microorganisms. It is named for French biochemist [[Jacques Monod]], who proposed using an equation of this form to relate microbial growth rates in an aqueous environment to the concentration of a limiting nutrient.<ref>{{cite journal |first=Jacques |last=Monod |year=1949 |title=The growth of bacterial cultures |journal=Annual Review of Microbiology |volume=3 |pages=371–394 |doi=10.1146/annurev.mi.03.100149.002103}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Monod |first=J. |year=1942 |title=Recherches sur la croissance des cultures bactériennes |lang=fr |publisher=Hermann |location=Paris }}</ref><ref>{{cite thesis |title=On-line parameter estimation, adaptative state estimation and adaptative control of fermentation processes |last=Dochain |first=D. |type=Thesis |publisher=[[Université catholique de Louvain]] |year=1986 |location=Louvain-la-Neuve, Belgium}}</ref> The Monod equation has the same form as the [[Michaelis–Menten kinetics|Michaelis–Menten equation]], but differs in that it is [[Empirical relationship|empirical]] while the latter is based on theoretical considerations.

The Monod equation is commonly used in [[environmental engineering]]. For example, it is used in the [[activated sludge model]] for [[sewage treatment]].

== Equation ==

[[Image:Monod 3.svg|thumb|upright|275px|The growth rate ''μ'' of a considered micro-organism as a function of the limiting substrate concentration [''S'']]]

The empirical Monod equation is<ref name="ESM 219">{{cite web |title=ESM 219: Lecture 5: Growth and Kinetics |url=http://www.bren.ucsb.edu/academics/courses/219/Lectures/Lecture_4_ESM219_06.ppt.pdf |archive-date=December 29, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091229043435/http://www.bren.ucsb.edu/academics/courses/219/Lectures/Lecture_4_ESM219_06.ppt.pdf }}</ref>

: <math> \mu = \mu_\max \frac{[S]}{K_s + [S]} </math>

where:
: ''μ'' is the growth rate of a considered microorganism,
: ''μ''<sub>max</sub> is the maximum growth rate of this microorganism,
: [''S''] is the concentration of the [[Limiting factor|limiting]] [[Enzyme substrate (biology)|substrate]] ''S'' for growth,
: ''K''<sub>''s''</sub> is the "half-velocity constant"—the value of [''S''] when ''μ''/''μ''<sub>max</sub> = 0.5.

''μ''<sub>max</sub> and ''K''<sub>''s''</sub> are empirical (experimental) coefficients to the Monod equation. They will differ between microorganism species and will also depend on the ambient environmental conditions, e.g., on the temperature, on the pH of the solution, and on the composition of the culture medium.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Graeme |first1=Walker M. |title=Yeast Physiology and Biotechnology |date=2000 |publisher=John Wiley & Sons |isbn=978-0-471-96446-9 |pages=59–60}}</ref>

== Application notes ==

The rate of substrate utilization is related to the specific growth rate as<ref>{{cite book |last1=Metcalf |first1=Eddy |year=2003 |title=Wastewater Engineering: Treatment & Reuse |edition=4th |publisher=McGraw–Hill |location=New York |isbn=0-07-041878-0 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=_iBSAAAAMAAJ }}</ref>

: <math>r_s = \mu X/Y,</math>
where
: ''X'' is the total biomass (since the specific growth rate ''μ'' is normalized to the total biomass),
: ''Y'' is the yield coefficient.

''r''<sub>''s''</sub> is negative by convention.

In some applications, several terms of the form [''S''] / (''K''<sub>''s''</sub>&nbsp;+&nbsp;[''S'']) are multiplied together where more than one nutrient or growth factor has the potential to be limiting (e.g. [[organic matter]] and [[oxygen]] are both necessary to [[heterotrophic]] bacteria). When the yield coefficient, being the ratio of mass of microorganisms to mass of substrate utilized, becomes very large, this signifies that there is deficiency of substrate available for utilization.

== Graphical determination of constants ==

As with the [[Michaelis–Menten kinetics|Michaelis–Menten equation]] graphical methods may be used to fit the coefficients of the Monod equation:<ref name="ESM 219" />

* [[Eadie–Hofstee diagram]]
* [[Hanes–Woolf plot]]
* [[Lineweaver–Burk plot]]
